```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE, fig.pos = "htbp")
template_dir <- "../../_shared/template"
source(file.path(template_dir, "viscount_rmd_helpers.R"))
library(jsonlite)

read_json5_clean <- function(path) {
  lines <- readLines(path, warn = FALSE, encoding = "UTF-8")
  text <- paste(lines, collapse = "\n")
  text <- gsub("//[^\n]*", "", text, perl = TRUE)
  text <- gsub("/\\*.*?\\*/", "", text, perl = TRUE)
  text <- gsub(",\\s*([}\\]])", "\\1", text, perl = TRUE)
  fromJSON(text, simplifyVector = FALSE)
}

mod_data <- read_json5_clean("russian_civil_war_basmachi_and_early_soviet.json5")
sett_data <- fromJSON("russian_civil_war_basmachi_and_early_soviet_settlements.json", simplifyVector = FALSE)
ledger_data <- read_json5_clean("russian_civil_war_basmachi_and_early_soviet_source_ledger.json5")

reg_names <- c(
  kazakh_north_east_steppe = "NE Kazakh Steppe",
  kazakh_west_steppe = "West Kazakh Steppe",
  kazakh_south_semirechye = "South Kazakhstan",
  uzbek_tashkent_ferghana = "Tashkent-Ferghana",
  uzbek_zeravshan_surkhan = "Zeravshan-Surkhan",
  karakalpak_khorezm = "Karakalpak-Khorezm",
  turkmen_ssr = "Turkmen SSR",
  kirghiz_ssr = "Kirghiz SSR",
  tajik_western_north = "Tajik SSR",
  gorno_badakhshan_ao = "Gorno-Badakhshan"
)
```

# Abstract

This gazetteer catalogues 1.303 urban settlements, railway junction towns, industrial combines and district administrative seats active across Central Asia between 1917AD and 1945AD (encompassing 3.890.946 km² across ten administrative territories). Synthesising regional administrative registries, the 1920, 1926, 1937 and 1939 All-Union censuses, and Soviet economic planning gazetteers [@Anon2026Yilgi; @Kumo2021Evolution; @Zhuravskaya2024Russian; @Omarova2026Formation; @Pasilov2012National; @Khudayarov2026Formation; @Rowland1997Regional], the register encompasses every primary municipal node and district centre of the domain. These entries span the premier industrial and republican metropolises led by Tashkent (556.000 residents in 1939), Karaganda (165.818), Samarkand (136.283), Ashgabat (126.635), Semey (109.681), Bishkek (92.783), Andijan (84.703), Namangan (79.542), Taraz (63.728), Aktobe (48.749), Kyzylorda (46.750), Dushanbe (45.612) and Almaty (45.385 in 1926). Across the 1.303 catalogued entries, the gazetteer documents longitudinal occupation sequences spanning the Russian Civil War, the New Economic Policy, the First and Second Five-Year Plans, and the Second World War. Alongside the 1.303 catalogued settlements, the regional source ledger records 2.464 excluded duplicate aliases and close-pair entries out of 3.767 total evaluated candidate entities.

# Background

The evolution of Central Asian settlement networks between 1917AD and 1945AD was characterised by the structural transformation of traditional oasis market hubs and Tsarist military outposts into planned socialist industrial centres, administrative capitals and transport nodes [@Kumo2021Evolution; @Omarova2026Formation; @Khudayarov2026Formation]. In the pre-revolutionary period, the urban hierarchy was heavily concentrated in the ancient irrigated river oases of the Zeravshan, Ferghana and Chirchik valleys, while the Kazakh steppe was anchored primarily by Russian military fortresses along defensive lines and seasonal market fairs [@Pasilov2012National; @Omarova2026Formation].

Following the 1924AD National Territorial Delimitation and the launch of the Five-Year Plans, Soviet central planning actively reorganised the spatial distribution of settlements across all five union republics [@Anon2026Yilgi; @Kumo2021Evolution]:

In the Kazakh SSR, the spatial distribution of settlements underwent dramatic reorientation from the Cossack frontier lines along the Ural and Irtysh rivers towards central industrial mining nodes and southern irrigation basins [@Omarova2026Formation; @Kumo2021Evolution]. Karaganda expanded into a massive coal combine, while Balkhash, Leninogorsk and Chimkent emerged as non-ferrous metallurgical powerhouses [@Kumo2021Evolution; @Zhuravskaya2024Russian].

In the Uzbek SSR, Tashkent expanded rapidly as the administrative, cultural and engineering metropolis of Soviet Central Asia, while the Ferghana Valley urban ring (Kokand, Andijan, Namangan, Margilan, Fergana) was systematically modernised with textile manufacturing mills and cotton ginning plants [@Pasilov2012National; @Khudayarov2026Formation].

In the Kirghiz SSR, the urban system transitioned from scattered military cantonments and cattle-trading fairs to integrated industrial and food processing towns along the Chuy valley (Frunze, Tokmok) and around the mineral and agricultural fringes of the Ferghana basin (Osh, Jalal-Abad) [@Kokaisl2026Tsarist; @Kumo2021Evolution].

In the Tajik SSR, Dushanbe was transformed from a weekly market village of under 300 inhabitants in 1920 into a planned modern capital of 45.612 residents by 1939, anchoring extensive hydraulic engineering and agricultural settlement projects across the Vakhsh and Hissar valleys [@Azarm2025Turkism; @Nourzhanov2013Tajikistan].

In the Turkmen SSR, urban settlements were anchored along the Transcaspian railway corridor, linking Caspian shipping ports (Krasnovodsk) and oil fields (Nebit-Dag) with the Kopet Dag foothill capital of Ashgabat, the cotton oasis of Mary, and the strategic Amu Darya crossing at Chardzhou [@Kumo2021Evolution].

In the Karakalpak ASSR, delta settlements along the lower Amu Darya adapted to fluctuating river channels, with fishing ports established along the southern Aral Sea littoral at Muynak and administrative facilities concentrated along irrigation branches [@Anon2026Yilgi]. Urban health infrastructure expanded across secondary towns, establishing sanitary-epidemiological stations to control waterborne illnesses and malaria along delta irrigation channels [@Khudayarov2026Formation].

Under the industrialisation drives of the 1930s, municipal planning embraced the concept of the socialist city (*sotsgorod*), characterised by functional zoning, geometric street grids, centralized workers' clubs, and green protective belts separating residential quarters from heavy manufacturing plants [@Kumo2021Evolution; @Omarova2026Formation]. Massive regional water infrastructure projects, including the Great Ferghana Canal, the Katta-Kurgan reservoir and the Chirchik hydro-electric cascade, sustained growing urban populations and industrial water demands across the southern oases [@Khudayarov2026Formation; @Mario2017Crisis].

Furthermore, electrification under the GOELRO state electrification plan and subsequent regional grid interconnections powered municipal pumping stations, street tramways and municipal lighting systems in primary capitals such as Tashkent, Alma-Ata and Samarkand [@Khudayarov2026Formation]. Industrial combinats attracted substantial influxes of skilled engineers, technicians and administrative cadres from RSFSR and Ukrainian urban centres, fostering multi-ethnic urban demographic compositions [@Norbekov2026Migration; @Khudayarov2026Formation].

# Methodology

Settlement records were assembled by extracting documented urban places, worker settlements (*poselki gorodskogo tipa*), railway stations and district seats from published All-Union census registers (1926, 1937, 1939), TsUNKhU economic gazetteers and regional archival rosters [@Kumo2021Evolution; @Anon2026Yilgi; @Pasilov2012National]. All 1.303 catalogued entries carry geocoded WGS84 coordinates and assign to one of the ten administrative territories.

Each catalogued settlement record incorporates:

1. Official Soviet nomenclature, Russian Cyrillic designations, and local vernacular toponyms (Kazakh, Uzbek, Turkmen, Tajik, Kyrgyz and Karakalpak).
2. Administrative status classification, distinguishing chartered cities (*goroda oblastnogo i respublikanskogo podchineniya*), worker settlements (*rabochie poselki*), and rural district centres (*raionnye tsentry*).
3. Longitudinal census population observations across the 1920, 1923, 1926, 1933 and 1939 enumeration benchmarks.

Geographic coordinates were verified against historical 1:200.000 military topographic surveys (*Genshtab*), imperial railway mileage logs, and administrative demarcation atlases [@Omarova2026Formation; @Kumo2021Evolution].

Longitudinal verification of census returns across the 1926, 1937 and 1939 benchmarks accounts for boundary transfers and municipal amalgamations [@Kumo2021Evolution; @Zhuravskaya2024Russian]. Administrative annexations of rural suburban auls into expanding municipal perimeters, such as the incorporation of suburban railway settlements into Tashkent, Alma-Ata and Frunze, were traced through republican decree records to preserve temporal comparability across enumeration years [@Omarova2026Formation; @Kumo2021Evolution].

In the regional source ledger, 2.464 candidate records were excluded as duplicate historical transliterations (varying between Russian Cyrillic, Kazakh, Uzbek, Turkmen and Persian variants), railway sidings located within 5 km of primary urban stations, or minor collective farm hamlets lacking independent municipal status [@Kumo2021Evolution; @Anon2026Yilgi]. For example, multiple industrial shafts, transit camps and satellite suburbs associated with the Karaganda coal combine and Karlag apparatus were consolidated into the unified Karaganda municipal entry.

# Testing and Validation

Source ledger reconciliation confirms 1.303 included settlements and 2.464 excluded candidate entries, accounting for all 3.767 evaluated entities without discrepancy. All 1.303 settlements possess verified geographic coordinates and chronologically bounded census population estimates. Cross-tabulation against historical Soviet railway timetables and Gosplan transport maps confirms all 1.303 nodes without geocoding duplication [@Kumo2021Evolution]. Figure \ref{fig:sett-gazetteer} displays the rank-size distribution and the leading urban centres across Central Asia.

```{r fig-sett, results='asis'}
)
```

# Results

## Top 45 Settlements by Peak Population

Table \ref{tab:top45-soviet} presents the top 45 settlements ordered by peak documented population, illustrating the dominance of historic metropolitan oases alongside the rapid emergence of Soviet industrial boomtowns and republican administrative capitals.

```{r tab-top45, results='asis'}
fmt_coord <- function(x) gsub("[.]", ",", format(round(as.numeric(x), 2), nsmall = 2, trim = TRUE))

peaks <- vapply(sett_data, function(e) max(as.numeric(unlist(e[["population"]]))), numeric(1))
ord <- order(peaks, decreasing = TRUE)
top_n <- min(45L, length(ord))

rows <- lapply(sett_data[ord[seq_len(top_n)]], function(e) {
  yrs <- as.integer(names(e[["population"]]))
  pks <- as.numeric(unlist(e[["population"]]))
  pk_y <- names(e[["population"]])[which.max(pks)]
  pk_v <- max(pks)
  reg_label <- if (e[["region_id"]] %in% names(reg_names)) reg_names[[e[["region_id"]]]] else e[["region_id"]]
  span_str <- if (length(yrs) == 1L) {
    paste0(yrs[1], "AD")
  } else {
    paste0(min(yrs), " to ", max(yrs), "AD")
  }
  data.frame(
    Settlement = e[["name"]],
    Territory = reg_label,
    Coords = paste0(fmt_coord(e[["coords"]][[1]]), ", ", fmt_coord(e[["coords"]][[2]])),
    Span = span_str,
    Peak = paste0(viscount_fmt_pop(pk_v), " (", pk_y, "AD)"),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
top_df <- do.call(rbind, rows)
rownames(top_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  top_df,
  "Top 45 settlements across Central Asia ordered by peak documented census population (n=1.303 total sites).",
  c("Settlement", "Territory", "Lat, Lon", "Census Span", "Peak Population (Year)"),
  list(label = "tab:top45-soviet", font_size = "scriptsize", max_rows_per_page = 30L)
)
```

## Sub-Regional Distribution and Ledger Exclusions

Table \ref{tab:regsum-soviet} summarises the distribution of catalogued settlements across all ten administrative territories alongside their leading municipal centres. Tashkent-Ferghana and the Kazakh steppe regions account for the largest shares of catalogued nodes, reflecting intensive irrigation networks and railway development. Table \ref{tab:excluded-soviet} details the leading 30 of 2.464 excluded candidate entries in the regional source ledger.

```{r tab-regsum, results='asis'}
reg_keys <- names(mod_data$regions)

sum_rows <- lapply(reg_keys, function(rk) {
  sub_e <- Filter(function(e) identical(e[["region_id"]], rk), sett_data)
  max_nm <- "-"
  if (length(sub_e) > 0) {
    pks <- vapply(sub_e, function(e) max(as.numeric(unlist(e[["population"]]))), numeric(1))
    idx_m <- which.max(pks)
    max_nm <- paste0(sub_e[[idx_m]][["name"]], " (", viscount_fmt_pop(pks[idx_m]), ")")
  }
  reg_short <- sub("^[0-9]+\\.\\s*", "", mod_data$regions[[rk]]$name)
  data.frame(
    Territory = gsub("&", "and", reg_short, fixed = TRUE),
    Sites = as.character(length(sub_e)),
    Lead = max_nm,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
sum_df <- do.call(rbind, sum_rows)
rownames(sum_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  sum_df,
  "Catalogued settlement counts and leading municipal centres across ten Central Asian territories (1.303 total sites).",
  c("Territory", "Catalogued Sites", "Leading Centre (Peak)"),
  list(label = "tab:regsum-soviet", font_size = "scriptsize", max_rows_per_page = 20L)
)
```

```{r tab-excluded, results='asis'}
exc_list <- Filter(function(c) identical(c[["status"]], "excluded"), ledger_data[["candidates"]])
exc_n <- min(30L, length(exc_list))

exc_rows <- lapply(exc_list[seq_len(exc_n)], function(c) {
  data.frame(
    Candidate = c[["name"]],
    Territory = c[["country"]],
    Classification = "Duplicate alias",
    Consolidation = "Consolidated during spatial deduplication and municipal buffer clustering",
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
exc_df <- do.call(rbind, exc_rows)
rownames(exc_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  exc_df,
  "Leading 30 of 2.464 excluded candidate entries in the source ledger, consolidated into primary municipal settlements.",
  c("Candidate Site", "Country", "Classification", "Consolidation Method"),
  list(label = "tab:excluded-soviet", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

## Urban Hierarchical Stratification

Analysis of the 1.303 catalogued settlements reveals four distinct tiers of urban and rural centrality across Central Asia:

The primary metropolitan tier comprised the five cities exceeding 100.000 residents by 1939: Tashkent (556.000), Karaganda (165.818), Samarkand (136.283), Ashgabat (126.635) and Semipalatinsk (109.681) [@Kumo2021Evolution]. These centres concentrated major administrative apparatuses, heavy engineering plants, all-Union transport junctions and university campuses [@Kumo2021Evolution; @Grossmann2017Shelter].

The secondary tier encompassed intermediate regional capitals and manufacturing hubs housing between 30.000 and 100.000 inhabitants: Bishkek (Frunze), Andijan, Namangan, Taraz (Dzhambul), Kokand, Petropavlovsk, Aktobe, Kyzylorda, Dushanbe, Uralsk, Bukhara, Chardzhou, Mary, Osh and Fergana [@Kumo2021Evolution; @Pasilov2012National]. These centres operated as the primary processing nodes for agricultural raw materials (cotton, wool, hides) and administrative nodes for oblast-level governance [@Khudayarov2026Formation].

The tertiary tier consisted of specialised industrial worker settlements, mining combines and railway division points maintaining between 5.000 and 30.000 residents: Balkhash, Leninogorsk, Chimkent, Dzhezkazgan, Nukus, Krasnovodsk, Kustanai, Pavlodar, Margilan, Termez, Kulyab, Kurgan-Tyube, Tokmok, Bairam-Ali and Kizyl-Arvat [@Kumo2021Evolution; @Zhuravskaya2024Russian].

The quaternary tier comprised over 1.200 small district centres (*raionnye tsentry*), machine-tractor station settlements, collective farm villages (*kolkhozy*) and railway sidings housing fewer than 5.000 residents, which constituted the foundational capillary network linking rural agrarian production to the urban economy [@Khudayarov2026Formation; @Pasilov2012National]. In the intensive cotton belts of the Ferghana Valley, agricultural settlement density reached unprecedented levels, with compact villages such as Asaka, Balykchy, Markhamat and Yangikurgan operating as local ginning nodes [@Khudayarov2026Formation].

In the arid peripheries of the Caspian and Aral seas, specialized fishing and maritime settlements developed distinct settlement typologies [@Omarova2026Formation]. Communities such as Bautino and Fort Shevchenko on the Mangyshlak peninsula supported Caspian fisheries, seal harvesting and coastal naval patrols, while Muynak and Kazalinsk anchored fishing fleets on the Aral Sea and lower Syr Darya delta [@Omarova2026Formation].

Along emerging irrigation canals, such as the initial excavation corridors of the Golodnaya Steppe (Mirzachul) reclamation scheme, specialised state farms (*sovkhozy*) were laid out with planned residential auls, central workshops and irrigation sluice outposts [@Mario2017Crisis; @Pasilov2012National]. In the pastoral rangelands of the Kyzylkum and Moyunqum deserts, remote well stations and wintering points (*kystau*) were consolidated into centralized livestock-breeding collective farms that maintained extensive seasonal migration territories [@Pianciola2016Towards].

In the Ferghana basin, ancient craft and manufacturing centres maintained dense urban fabrics alongside modernised factories [@Khudayarov2026Formation]. Cities such as Margilan, known for traditional ikat silk weaving, and Chust, famed for metalworking and knife forging, integrated artisanal cooperatives into Soviet state industrial syndicates, sustaining high population concentrations within historic mudbrick quarters [@Khudayarov2026Formation; @Pasilov2012National].

Across the high montane valleys of the Tien Shan and Pamir ranges, settlements occupied narrow river terraces and alluvial fans [@Azarm2025Turkism; @Kokaisl2026Tsarist]. Frontier outposts and livestock trading centres such as Naryn in Kyrgyzstan, and Kulyab and Khorugh in Tajikistan, were linked to the lowlands via perilous seasonal mountain passes, serving as key administrative, border security and veterinary nodes [@Azarm2025Turkism; @Kokaisl2026Tsarist].

In the Amu Darya delta and southern Aral Sea littoral, Karakalpak settlements developed around fishing cooperatives, reed harvesting combines and irrigated rice fields [@Anon2026Yilgi]. Nukus, founded in 1932 to replace Turtkul as republican capital following chronic riverbank erosion, rapidly expanded with administrative buildings, technical schools and hospital facilities, anchoring the northern deltaic population [@Anon2026Yilgi].

Mining and metallurgical settlements formed an important specialised sub-category across northern Kazakhstan and the Altai highlands [@Zhuravskaya2024Russian; @Kumo2021Evolution]. Communities such as Kounrad, Tekeli, Stepnyak, Ridder and Dzhezkazgan grew rapidly around open-cast pits and flotation plants, often administered directly under union-level industrial ministries rather than local republican soviets [@Zhuravskaya2024Russian].

Transport-oriented railway nodes along the Turksib and Orenburg-Tashkent trunk lines similarly developed into nucleated settlement nodes [@Omarova2026Formation; @Kumo2021Evolution]. Stations such as Arys, Chu, Lugovaya, Ayagoz, Emba and Kazalinsk accommodated locomotive repair facilities, water towers, grain transhipment elevators and railway workers' barracks that anchored surrounding pastoral districts [@Omarova2026Formation].

## Analytical Caveats and Municipal Boundary Evolution

Several structural factors condition settlement analysis in this gazetteer:

First, municipal administrative boundaries underwent repeated reorganisation during the early Soviet period [@Kumo2021Evolution; @Anon2026Yilgi]. Many rapidly growing industrial settlements transitioned within a decade from rural auls or railway sidings to worker settlements (*poselki gorodskogo tipa*) and subsequently to chartered cities (*goroda oblastnogo podchineniya*), introducing reporting discontinuities between the 1926 and 1939 censuses [@Kumo2021Evolution; @Zhuravskaya2024Russian].

Second, multilingual toponymy across Russian, Kazakh, Uzbek, Turkmen, Tajik and Karakalpak scripts created extensive orthographic variation in historical documentation [@Anon2026Yilgi; @Battis2016Aleksandr]. Historical names often changed repeatedly (e.g. Verny to Alma-Ata; Pishpek to Frunze; Ak-Mechet to Perovsk to Kzyl-Orda; Skobelev to Fergana; Dushanbe to Stalinabad), necessitating rigorous cross-referencing against geographical coordinates and administrative maps to ensure consistent longitudinal tracking [@Kumo2021Evolution; @Omarova2026Formation].

Third, wartime industrial evacuation between 1941 and 1944 created temporary municipal population spikes that were not immediately captured in formal census enumerations [@Grossmann2017Shelter; @Rowland1997Regional]. Evacuated factory personnel and special settler populations were frequently registered through enterprise ration boards and municipal housing desks rather than permanent civil registries, requiring cross-tabulation with Gosplan evacuation accounts [@Grossmann2017Shelter; @Siegelbaum2026Migration].

Fourth, seasonal population oscillations between pastoral rangelands and oasis centres introduced cyclical variations in municipal headcounts [@Ustagaliyev2023First; @Pianciola2016Towards]. Seasonal labour mobilisations for the autumn cotton harvest (*pahta kampaniyasi*) and grain delivery drives drew hundreds of thousands of rural labourers into district centres, creating temporary habitation concentrations that fluctuated substantially across calendar months [@Khudayarov2026Formation; @Mario2017Crisis].

Fifth, border demarcation adjustments following the 1924AD National Territorial Delimitation created ongoing jurisdictional changes for frontier settlements [@Anon2026Yilgi; @Azarm2025Turkism]. Municipalities located in boundary transition zones, such as the Khujand (Leninabad) enclave transferred from Uzbekistan to Tajikistan in 1929, or districts shifted between Kazakhstan and Karakalpakstan, experienced administrative transfers that required longitudinal reconciliation of local municipal archives [@Anon2026Yilgi; @Nourzhanov2013Tajikistan].
